Yet the disruption of Trump’s festivities </span><span>is</span><span> a harbinger of many disruptions to come. The brutal heat wave in the northeastern US — an event that would have been “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3db28ddf-25ac-4fbf-85e3-05c2041e8ae5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">virtually impossible</a><span>” without climate change — followed an even more brutal heat wave in Europe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These disasters represent the leading edge of serious damage — social, human, and economic — from a warming planet.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Projections of future climate change are often expressed in terms of averages: </span><span>B</span><span>y 2050 average global temperatures are expected to be </span><span>above pre-industrial levels by around</span><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/43d01704-cbc1-4305-b41a-bbf4592994d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">2.5° C</a><span> — 4 ½ degrees Fahrenheit</span><span>,</span><span> while sea levels will </span><span>be</span><span> 10 inches</span><span>higher</span><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should all </span><span>treat these predictions as highly credible. Although</span><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5e221bfe-7a2a-47ac-a586-b0a0c80b8820?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>fossil-fuel-financed climate denialism</span></a><span> </span><span>pervades right-wing politics and media, climate scientists who warned decades ago about future warming have been overwhelmingly vindicated</span><span>. Indeed, in many cases their predictions have closely matched the actual numbers. So w</span><span>hen </span><span>climate scientists </span><span>predict much more warming ahead, we should believe them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Focusing on </span><span>the </span><span>average </span><span>temperature increase</span><span> can, however, lead people to </span><span>underestimate </span><span>the damage that lies ahead. If the typical day is a few degrees warmer, if the waves on a typical day </span><span>are </span><span>a few inches higher, </span><span>what’s the big deal?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The </span><span>rejoinder </span><span>is that what may look like a modest change in these averages implies a large change in the risk of </span><span>extreme weather events. </span><span>A few degrees of average warming </span><span>correspond to </span><span>a huge increase in the frequency of heat emergencies like the ones we just saw on both sides of the Atlantic. A few inches added to sea levels </span><span>corresponds to </span><span>a huge rise in the probability of catastrophic storm surges.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And these extreme events </span><span>are exacting </span><span>an ever-growing human and economic toll. The U.S. toll was smaller, although </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0542bd51-190c-4ee7-9063-245752e295cc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">not zero</a><span>, </span><span>because our heat wave was less severe and because of the pervasiveness of air conditioning. </span><span>Yet w</span><span>e are facing a future in which </span><span>death</span><span> and destruction </span><span>from extreme weather events are certain to rise everywhere as the planet continues to warm.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inevitably, t</span><span>he economic costs of climate change are also certain to rise. But they’re polluting, and at least some analysts are warning that supply shortages may lead to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8cadb490-e33b-4446-9eee-2dd6c5b2d90b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">rising gas prices</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In addition to doing all it can to accelerate climate change, the Trump administration is actively placing Americans at risk by shuttering programs that help the nation prepare and recover from climate change catastrophes. Deep cuts to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9b3cc1bf-15d3-4591-aed0-e0da18fd59ff?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">FEMA and the National Weather Service</a><span>, along with cuts for programs that help </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4a0bd2fd-b546-4880-9a80-6a0e917480ae?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>build resilience</span></a><span>, will inevitably leave Americans poorer and undermine communities. It’s like burning down the hospital because you don’t like the diagnosis.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And did you hear about last week’s Thermostat War? It wasn’t a huge incident in itself, but it was, I believe, deeply revealing about how political dysfunction will undermine our response to climate change.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s what happened: During the heat emergency, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani urged the city’s residents to limit the burden on the grid by keeping their air conditioners at 78 degrees. Right-wing commentators went wild, denouncing his request as left-wing extremism — apparently only Communists believe in conserving energy during a crisis. But MS-NOW, among other media outlets, quickly noted that Mamdani’s suggestion echoed longstanding federal guidance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And the Department of Energy immediately closed down its web pages offering that guidance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whether we want to acknowledge it or not, climate change is going to impose large economic costs, some of which are already baked — and I mean baked — in. But the Trump administration’s rejection of both science and basic energy economics, along with vandalism of programs meant to help Americans prepare and survive climate catastrophes, will make the damage to America much worse than it should have been.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MUSICAL CODA</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a1a30891-e544-46d4-b921-d97f1dea1a1e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/WS_YAKZH3lw" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. with Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/66d74309-c988-42c3-b489-815530840521?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">NurPhoto</a><span>/Contributor via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">About a month ago, I found myself asked to speak on a panel about the crisis of the global center-left and struggling a little to think of something new to say. What occurred to me is that in the spirit of “the exception that proves the rule,” it might be useful to approach the question from the opposite direction and think about Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is running what seems to be clearly the most successful center-left political party in the world right now. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The idea of the exception that proves the rule is not that the existence of an exception demonstrates that a rule is true. It’s that if you lay down a rule (“the center-left is in crisis globally”) and then find an apparent exception (“the Liberal Party of Canada is doing great”), this </span><em>tests</em><span> what the rule actually is and lets you rephrase it more precisely. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In other words, if we understand what’s distinctive about Carney — or about the Liberal Party or about Canada — we can better understand what’s happening everywhere else. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note that what is impressive about Carney’s political achievements isn’t just that he won an election. Joe Biden and Keir Starmer also won elections. I know a lot of people on Bluesky think Starmer’s collapse debunks popularism and all the rest. But I think it mostly just goes to show that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1843fcd4-e86f-4f42-8f87-e2abf7a0ec43?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the popularism debate is over and boring</a><span> because popularism is obviously correct and that the most interesting and difficult question is how to actually govern a country. That’s where Biden and Starmer both struggled. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unlike them, Carney didn’t just win. He has maintained a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f9ac09c-3ca4-4b29-8d1d-0097355a5332?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">net positive </a><span>approval rating and put the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0a44113b-6fa3-450e-8faf-5e95e359197d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Liberals on track to win a new election</a><span>. He also persuaded several members of Parliament to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9158d0f1-e4fd-41dd-b23e-ab799075ef11?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">switch parties and join the Liberals</a><span>, helping take his government from a minority to a majority. And what makes this even more impressive is that the Liberals have been in power, mostly under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, since November of 2015. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My read of this situation is that some of the successes are tactical points that more or less everyone could learn from relatively easily and apply elsewhere. But a structural factor that’s harder to copy is that the Liberal Party has a different kind of relationship to Canada than you see from most center-left parties around the world. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Canada is a country whose existence has been repeatedly contested throughout history, whose statehood could have evaporated at various points in the past, and whose place on the map might vanish someday. The Liberals, more than any other force in Canadian politics, are the </span><em>national</em><span> party of Canada — they’re the party that says it’s good that Canada is up there, the true north strong and free. The particulars of Donald Trump’s assault on Canadian sovereignty re-engaged that mentality. That’s not just an electoral shot in the arm; it gives the Liberals a mission and purpose and a way of thinking about policy choices and relating to voters that most center-left parties around the world really struggle with. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe Augello</a><span>/Variety via Getty Images</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To get this story right, I think you need to start with the point that even though Trudeau left office unpopular, he is probably the most successful politician of our time. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a democracy, nobody stays on top forever. But Trudeau took over as leader of a once-great political party that had fallen into third place and was plausibly going to go the way of the old Liberal Party of the United Kingdom. Instead, he led them to three electoral victories. He governed for nine and a half years, and when he stepped aside he did so in favor of a fellow Liberal, Carney, who proceeded to win an election on his own and then improve the Liberals’ standing through the aforementioned floor-crossings. This kind of successful transfer of power is extremely hard to pull off. It’s what made Ronald Reagan and F.D.R. such titans of 20th-century American politics, and it’s why Barack Obama, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8dfcad29-23da-4c50-b99c-9ba97685e205?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">though he mostly got things right</a><span>, ultimately left a shallower legacy than he should have. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s true, of course, that Carney’s political success has come in part from breaking with Trudeau on key issues. He rescinded the unpopular Trudeau-era consumer carbon tax and has moved to sharply cut immigration after it surged under his predecessor. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the very short term, this can make Trudeau look like a failure whose successor has done well purely by repudiating him. Zoom out, though, and you see that Trudeau’s cash benefit for low-income kids is still in place. So are the expansions of Canadian Medicare to include dental benefits and prescription drugs. The repealed and unpopular consumer carbon tax was not having a large impact on emissions. The bulk of the work of Trudeau’s climate plan was done by the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b14ddf99-4c63-4a34-b04c-255e8ebcda87?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">industrial carbon tax</a><span>, which was (and is) less salient to consumers and remains in place. On immigration, the Stephen Harper-to-Trudeau-to-Carney seesaw is going to leave what was already one of the most open countries on Earth more open to immigration than it was before the Liberal win in 2015 — hopefully in a sustainable, controlled, and selective way. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Getting squeezed out of power must have hurt Trudeau’s feelings on a number of levels. And unlike Kamala Harris, Carney really did vocally break with him in several ways and credibly position himself as an agent of change. But in doing so, he secured Trudeau’s legacy and set him off to travel the world with Katy Perry. </p><p class="button-wrapper" optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Tactical lessons from Canada</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A big part of what happened here, I think, is that Canadian Liberals learned some valuable tactical lessons from the failures of American Democrats. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Trudeau’s case there was no question of incapacity or coverup or scandal; it was just that he was unpopular and clearly going to lose the election, so he got dumped as leader. The challenge to him came in the first instance from Chrystia Freeland, a senior member of his government who had served in various cabinet roles over the years. Freeland used to be a D.C.-based journalist, is well-known globally, and I think was broadly positioned as “next in line” to lead the Liberals. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But, </span><em>again</em><span> learning a lesson from the United States, the Liberals ditched not only the unpopular leader but also the natural successor. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem with Freeland, after all, is that if Trudeau’s unpopularity was the problem then replacing him with a senior member of his cabinet doesn’t really solve anything. My intuition, trained on the mechanics of the Democratic Party, was that there was no way a well-qualified woman who clearly </span><em>deserved</em><span> the leadership based on service and history was going to get shoved aside in favor of a less-qualified man. And the Liberals I’ve spoken to about this really did feel bad about Freeland losing her opportunity. But they felt that they had to be tough-minded rather than sentimental. Pierre Poilievre and the Conservatives had real weaknesses, but to exploit those weaknesses the Liberals needed to position themselves as offering a form of change. That was easier to do with Carney, so they picked Carney. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Their choice was a contrast with recent Democratic Party decision-making on another level. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Carney — like John F. Kennedy, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton, and Barack Obama — was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/14973aff-26a7-4aa2-80a7-4a3dede13765?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">an outsider to Ottawa and Canadian party politics but not a radical</a><span>. This is the magic formula for progressive political parties: fresh faces and good government and reform </span><em>without</em><span> hard-left ideology. Democrats keep acting as if the only options are the most tedious time-serving establishment warriors and radical leftists. But Canada reminds us that party leaders can be tough-minded and look beyond their own insular cliques to find talent and win. But what’s most impressive about Carney isn’t his electoral win; it’s the staying power of his popularity. And for that you need to look beyond tactics to strategy. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The Canadian party </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Canada is a bit of a weird country. When it was a British colony, the United States tried to conquer it repeatedly. Granted, there’s a kind of obvious logic to the large English-speaking former British colony absorbing the adjacent English-speaking British colony. Of course, not all of Canada is English-speaking. But that’s odd, too. For Canada to today be </span><em>neither</em><span> a British colony </span><em>nor</em><span> annexed by the United States </span><em>nor</em><span> divided along linguistic lines into separate countries is a bit like paddling upstream. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And a big part of the story the Liberal Party tells about itself is that it is less ideological than most modern political parties around the world, in part precisely because it is a party that is dedicated to that difficult paddling mission. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not that only the Liberal Party has supported Canada qua Canada throughout Canadian history. But the Liberals have been most distinctively dedicated to it. In the 19th century they were the more anti-imperialist party. They became the party that was more interested in conciliating Francophone concerns. They were the party that crafted the Constitution Act of 1982 and formally secured total Canadian autonomy from Britain. By contrast, the Progressive Conservative Party under Brian Mulroney won big majorities along the lines of Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, but (unlike other Anglophone center-right parties) regional differences of opinion tore it apart and it no longer exists. A Canadian center-right was eventually reconstituted, but that happened by embracing a destiny as a party of western grievance politics. The left-wing New Democratic Party reached its </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83bd1cdc-ea3a-480a-89f5-72d575644629?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">high-water mark in 2011</a><span> by dominating Francophone seats.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The </span><em>Liberals</em><span> are the party that is focused on keeping the country from flying apart and keeping it independent. That meant the crisis induced by Donald Trump trolling about turning Canada into the 51st state played right into their core competency of doing what it takes to win and save Canada. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Patriots and pragmatists</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One part of this is just that the Liberals do a better job than contemporary center-left parties in most countries of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02b77ebc-2ef6-41c7-ae98-d9c2de1427ef?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">embracing patriotism and positivity about their country</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Canadian patriotism can seem a little funny to Americans at times because it’s a kind of very non-nationalistic patriotism grounded in the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cfe70558-a6e9-4022-9537-57cc01d949a5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">mosaic, not melting pot</a><span>” vision of multiculturalism. It’s hard to imagine an American political ad thoroughly rooted in patriotism also being as ironic and jokey as this Carney ad. But it’s </span><em>also</em><span> hard to imagine an American Democrat running an ad that is so comprehensively situated in patriotism and national identity and celebration of the country’s quirks. </span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/494ae9f0-544d-4174-af32-9605583501c1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/al9yWA4TUII" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Patriotism is smart politics, but jokes about the Tragically Hip do not win elections alone. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What I think is really critical here is that sincere belief in the Liberals’ mission of national salvation has allowed Carney to be a bit cynical. He pivoted hard away from some unpopular Trudeau commitments on climate and immigration. He’s brokered new energy deals with Alberta. He’s done the kind of stuff that people like me are always saying Democrats should do. But notably he’s also not getting a ton of blowback the way a Democrat who moved this decisively would. He’s also not dogged by allegations of being “inauthentic” or excessively calculating and poll-tested even as he does a bunch of poll-tested stuff that’s calculated to win. That’s because there’s a kind of meta-earnestness behind the cynicism — just as, for all the jokiness of the Mike Myers ad, they’re actually deadly serious about the ongoing existence of Canada being on the line. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Democrats have done a lot of existential threat rhetoric during the Trump era, but it’s always rung pretty hollow. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Not because all the Orange Man Bad stuff is insincere, per se, but because it’s just clearly always taken a bit of a back seat to other considerations, including to dozens of different interest-group advocacy campaigns and also this long factional struggle playing out between “the establishment” and Bernie Sanders and his followers. This happens because the Democrats are, historically, an interest-group coalition party that slowly over the past two generations has been transforming into an ideological progressive party. It’s not an un-American party or an anti-patriotic one or whatever slanders the right might direct at it, but it’s certainly not an aggressively patriotic party. If you see a person flying a flag on his lawn, your guess is going to be that he’s a Republican. This is an electoral handicap on its own terms but also a bit of an impediment to certain kinds of solidaristic projects — including calls for electoral pragmatism. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The nation and the state </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back to where we started with the problems of the global center-left: I think an issue here beyond any specific election is that parties of the center-left are committed to being parties of </span><em>the state</em><span> and specifically parties of the government’s taxing function. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not a big mystery how that came to be the case — the existing social safety net was largely created by the center-left. Where it was created by the right, that was normally an effort to preempt more progressive forces. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But those welfare states were also largely created by earlier, more patriotic and nationalistic iterations of center-left political parties. After all, part of the idea of redistribution and solidarity is that we all owe something to each other as members of the same national community. This is a totally reasonable idea and it’s not a coincidence that defending the existing safety net is Democrats’ most popular version of themselves. But the idea of a state whose function is to fulfill our mutual obligations to each other doesn’t make a lot of sense unless you also value the national community that the state governs. In a European context, maybe you can imagine a post-national progressive politics coming out on the other side as a forceful advocate for a European super-state full of Euro-patriot followers who wave the E.U. flag — though I would say witnessing everyone’s fervent attachments to their national teams during the World Cup makes me doubt how plausible that is. Here in America, meanwhile, there’s just no viable post-national option at all. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That doesn’t mean you have to become a frothing-at-the-mouth demagogue who’s talking about conquering Canada or Greenland. And it also doesn’t mean you need to become a paranoid xenophobe who thinks immigrants are destroying the country or has a zero-sum view of world trade. But you do need a real sense of being a </span><em>national</em><span> party that believes in your country qua country as something worth fighting for. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><strong>Transcript</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today i want to give you some encouraging news about the state of the heartland. Well, actually New Jersey, but you got a problem with that? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I did something kind of different yesterday — which has prevented me from producing a usual analytical Substack post — and it was actually a very uplifting experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So hi, I’m Paul Krugman. What i did yesterday was participate in jury selection in Mercer County, New Jersey, where i am still a legal resident.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That is something I’ve done before: back in 2020 I spent 16 weeks on a grand jury. It was done remotely, because it was the depths of Covid. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was a New Jersey grand jury, which is not high profile cases. It’s actually very ordinary cases in which the police want to bring someone to trial but 23 citizens must agree that they have provided sufficient evidence to bring the case to trial. You don’t have to judge guilt or innocence but you have to judge that there is sufficient evidence to warrant bringing charges. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was enlightening. I got to see a lot of the negative side of life, obviously, but it was just it was a pretty good experience on the whole.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So I was summoned again this year. I wouldn’t have been able to do it, but I had to participate in the selection in order to explain to the judge, if necessary, why I could not be available during the period of this grand jury — a bunch of already agreed to conferences and talks in Europe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So it wasn’t going to be something I could do, but I did the right thing and went through the whole procedure of listening to the explanation, being pronounced present, and waiting to see the judge and explain the issue. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, as it turned out, I didn’t even have to do that. By the time they had reached the people who had said they could not do it, including me and 77 other people, they already had filled the jury. So it ended up that it was time-consuming, okay, not a terrible thing, but it was a procedure that had to be done. And I did my citizenly duty and was released well into the afternoon.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But what was interesting about it was that those of us who had said we couldn’t do it — 78 people in a Zoom room — had a long wait while the judge did whatever she needed to do with the rest. And after a little while some people unmuted themselves and we started having a conversation. This was by definition kind of a random sample of people — of course people who have felony convictions are not part of this, people are not us citizens are not part of it, and to be fair it’s Mercer County which includes Princeton although it also includes Trenton. Still, it’s on average an affluent, highly educated county so this was not exactly typical America but it wasn’t exactly the elite either: This wasn’t a virtual room full of Princeton professors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So conversation started. Obviously people are not fools so it wasn’t about politics, it wasn’t about current events, it started with people saying “anybody want to recommend some books that I should read?” and then turned to TV shows and movies and then somehow or other we got involved in a discussion of AI and applications and learning. Because there were several school teachers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not everyone spoke up — most people didn’t — but everyone was listening, it seemed fairly attentively. And it was a great conversation! People were reasonable, they were either well informed or were happy to say “I don’t know about this.” There was actually some discussion about “how should I where should I go for news now that everything is so polarized” — nobody talked politics but they did talk about the fact that news is kind of hard to parse these days.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The book recommendations, the TV and movie recommendations to the extent that I know them were pretty good. And the whole tone was, wow, it was civilized. I felt a little bit as if I was in the middle of a Norman Rockwell painting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By the way, yes, people did recognize me and a couple said you know I read your Substack and I talked a little bit but I made a deliberate effort to step back and not play the celebrity there.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And that was good, because I got to listen to other people who were really level-headed, interesting, pretty well informed about a bunch of stuff. Oh, and just to say that this was New Jersey, so it was a very diverse group of people — a random selection of people from New Jersey, which meant that it was multi-racial and multi-ethnic. The clerk had some trouble with pronouncing everybody’s name, which was okay — I mean everybody was very forgiving of that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So it was very much America as I see it — a country of lots of people who look very different, who sound different (except a fair number of people did have New Jersey accents.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it was just a far more hopeful scene — at least I found it much more hopeful —about the state of the country. It turns out that ordinary Americans — this is, again ordinary Americans from Mercer County, New Jersey, but still — ordinary Americans are a lot nicer, more thoughtful, more willing to hold interesting discussions than you might think.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it does seem to me, given all the political news, there’s a lot of people out there, I would say primarily on the right, but not only on the right, who fundamentally hold ordinary Americans in contempt, who believe that you have to go with cheap slogans and that you can appeal to the baser instincts of everybody’s nature and that’s the way that you win.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And obviously they do sometimes win. But it’s worth going out there a little bit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I mean I’m never going to be the kind of person who travels around and has conversations with the person in the street and reports back on what I’ve learned about the real America. But I actually did have, by accident, a pretty good selection of real Americans — because we’re all real Americans — and came out of it feeling just much lighter in mood. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You know, this country is actually okay if we can just get past some of the people who are trying to take us down a dark path. We’re not bad people — we’re mostly good people. And there’s a lot there’s a lot of uplift out here if you’re willing to see it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For once if I say I’m ending on a happy note, I really am.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Take care.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. The donkey is the unofficial mascot of the Democratic Party. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/78ce94d3-6d30-459b-9acd-c19eee5fb87d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>imageBROKER/Frank Sommariva</span></a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now that the Graham Platner Era appears to be in our rearview mirror, I think an important point to make about this episode has nothing to do with the scandal that brought him down. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The point is that polls, as Greg Sargent wrote during the campaign, showed Platner </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cfe56856-849c-42ca-8c69-f289626be187?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">trailing badly with non-college voters</a><span> even while he was beating Susan Collins handily with Maine college graduates. That’s not particularly surprising — he’s a Democrat running against a Republican in a state with almost no African Americans and all kinds of Democrats run weak with non-college whites. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the lack of surprise is the point. There’s a big faction of Democrats who are absolutely convinced that if you pound the table hard enough with Bernie/Warren economics that you’ll win non-college voters. Then there’s an identity-obsessed sub-faction that acknowledges this doesn’t really work but thinks that if you cast the perfect gruff white man you can make it work and Platner was supposed to be their perfect gruff white man. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And the thing is, he really might have beaten Collins absent the scandal — not because of any special working-class appeal, but because Maine is a state Kamala Harris won pretty handily in a bad national year for Democrats.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The truth is we know the names of the Democrats who do well with working-class voters. They’re Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez</span><strong> </strong><span>in the rural north. They’re Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez in South Texas. They’re Josh Shapiro and Gretchen Whitmer and Elissa Slotkin in the Rust Belt. They’re Ruben Gallego and Mark Kelly and Katie Hobbs in Arizona. People knock these candidates as too boring, but the truth is that a network of political operatives and sympathetic media figures were incredibly successful at </span><em>generating</em><span> enthusiasm for Platner because </span><em>they</em><span> felt enthusiastic about the </span><em>idea</em><span> of Graham Platner. Which is fine. But if they chose to get excited by — and spread excitement about — people who are actually good at beating Republicans, then Democrats would have a lot less trouble making those candidates seem exciting. </span></p><div class="subscription-widget-wrap" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="subscription-widget show-subscribe" style="font-size: 16px;direction: ltr !important;font-weight: 400;text-decoration: none;font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';color: #363737;line-height: 1.5;max-width: 560px;margin: 24px auto;align-items: flex-start;display: block;text-align: center;padding: 0px 32px;"><div class="preamble" style="margin-top: 16px;font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-size: 18px;max-width: 384px;width: fit-content;line-height: 22px;display: flex;align-items: center;text-align: center;font-weight: 400;margin-left: auto;margin-right: auto;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Mailbag is free for everyone, but paid subscribers asked the questions below. href="https://substack.com/redirect/877907bf-1e02-4a31-abf1-c6edf95637f0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>claimed in his recent Vox piece</span></a><span> that abundance seems to be failing as a tool for building factional power for moderates. What is your theory of the case for making the “Promise to America” project succeed, and what can actually be done differently? When Jonathan Karl asked Mamdani about the moderate manifesto, he seemed to swat it away effortlessly, implicitly casting moderate Dems as scolding manifesto-writers while he is out there “delivering”. Ritchie Torres, OG abundance guy, in an interview last week described Mamdani’s synthesis of populism and abundance as something he aspires to. In fact, Torres wouldn’t even criticize the ill advised rent freeze. Auchincloss, another abundance star, is facing a credible primary challenger over Israel. Meanwhile, Josh Gottheimer becoming a face of the mod project feels like a major optics problem. Is there more appealing young talent out there capable of leading the mod faction successfully?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think this take involves conflating a lot of different things. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Abundance, in practice, is mostly the YIMBY movement and the YIMBY movement continues to be an incredible success story on a policy level. My only real criticism of YIMBYism as a tendency is that it’s excessively self-critical. There is all this </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d2f2793-6918-44bc-b40e-a6c9f40fcd5c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">constant concern-trolling of what YIMBYs are getting wrong</a><span>, but YIMBYs have passed a ton of bills in state legislatures, a bunch of local reforms, and now a landmark piece of federal housing legislation. It’s true that not every YIMBY reform has been effective, but some of them have. And precisely because a lot of reforms have passed, YIMBYs are able to learn from experience and focus more effort over time on better proposals. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Abundance, as a policy concept, continues to have the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b1d4e86-606c-4b3c-a5db-52207919edf1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">half-drawn horse problem I wrote about last fall</a><span> — housing abundance is really robust, energy abundance has ideas and some legislative momentum, and then beyond that it gets really sketchy fast. Which is just to say there’s a lot of work to be done. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Moderate factional organizing inside the Democratic Party very partially overlaps with abundance, but they are not the same thing. I think the overlap is great. I, personally, am in it, I think Slow Boring is in it, and if you come to one of our happy hours, you’ll find yourself surrounded by people who are in it. But these are different ideas. Most abundance legislation is, in practice, bipartisan. Bipartisan legislation tends to appeal to members from frontline districts. And members from frontline districts naturally have an interest in moderate factional organizing, so that’s another place where there’s overlap. But </span><em>by definition</em><span> bipartisan legislation and factional moderate partisanship are different ideas.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One consequence is that it also wouldn’t really make sense to try to gatekeep abundance and say that Zohran Mamdani isn’t allowed to make zoning reform a priority. I did think it was a mistake of D.C.-area YIMBY activists to be </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/46cfb32f-a22e-4455-b155-740e8fa76946?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">so credulous about Janeese Lewis George</a><span>, but if she proves me wrong by delivering a big increase in housing production I’ll be thrilled. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the thing I say any time I’m invited to secret factional scheming is that the main reason abundance doesn’t work as a factional pillar is that it’s too far removed from the main issues in public opinion. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Being bipartisan and being in some sense “pro-business” are both politically good for Democrats. But the barrier to Democrats winning more elections is that lots of voters think the party is dominated by culturally alien weirdos who practice anti-white racial discrimination, won’t enforce the law, and have bizarre beliefs about sex and gender. The best Republican issues are ones that hit on multiple topics, like Democrats are soft on illegal immigration because they hate enforcing the law and also want to do a great replacement of white people. Or (per Trump’s ad) Democrats have both weird ideas about gender identity and also are soft on crime, so they want government-funded sex-change operations for convicts. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The most common failure mode for contemporary Democrats is believing that if they somehow get the economic messaging just right then people will stop caring about those cultural issues. But clearly Democrats themselves care a great deal about these issues and that’s why they are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f985eb3b-9b33-42f7-a5bf-ee84e9c0ca7b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">so reluctant to compromise with public opinion</a><span> on them. If Democrats are allowed to care a lot, so are swing voters. But I think a niche subset of Democrats wants to make the same mistake in reverse and say that if the party embraces “abundance,” that will scratch the itch for being different without taking on the actual electorally relevant sacred cows. Rob Sand in Iowa just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c88dcb0-f4d1-4225-9032-5b8838fd03d2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">taking the popular position on girls’ sports teams</a><span> or James Talarico saying he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/72e60434-e74f-41ba-846c-d127bddba8df?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">likes the Texas oil and gas industry</a><span> is politics with real impact. The energy heterodoxy arguably fits in the abundance frame, but if it does </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73563894-4dd5-431f-b503-fad90c764832?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">it’s Big-Ass Truck Abundance</a><span> and not high-speed-rail abundance. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If I got to puppetmaster all of moderate politics (which sadly I do not) the two core principles would be:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Helping the poor</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">A big tent on culture</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The former distinguishes moderate Democrats from Republicans, of course. But it also distinguishes moderate Democrats from degrowth eco-fanatics and the really toxic strands of socialism and neo-Brandeisianism that center hurting the rich over lifting up the poor. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The latter I mean in a much more robust way than most current moderate Democrats. I think that on questions of broad moral and cultural values, politicians should try to mirror their constituents, not aggressively lead them. I think someone like Scott Wiener who is very left-wing on culture but also represents San Francisco should be a welcome voice in moderate circles but that we should </span><em>also</em><span> be finding a cohort of politicians like John Bel Edwards to run in states like Louisiana. My personal views are between Wiener and Edwards, but their views reflect the places where they live. With location-appropriate cultural politics in place, you can then try to do good economic policy — whether that means housing abundance in San Francisco or Medicaid expansion in Louisiana — to make people’s lives better in a pragmatic and thoughtful way. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What I would ask of everyone at the table is simply that they respect the diversity of America and the wisdom of trying to compete effectively across this vast and varied land rather than trying to cancel each other. And I would urge people whose passion in life is </span><em>shifting public opinion</em><span> rather than responding to it to find a different line of work than electoral politics. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=288914927" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Marcus Seldon:</a><span> Let’s say Obama was more politically restrained in his second term and doesn’t try to enact DAPA or the clean power plan. Would this have been enough for Hillary to win in 2016? Or even have prevented Trump from building a coalition large enough to win the GOP primary?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hillary Clinton lost by a very narrow margin, so it’s plausible to construct all kinds of but-for counterfactuals where relatively small changes lead to her winning. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t necessarily think that Barack Obama being more restrained would have accomplished that, though, because the dynamic of the 2016 race was to consistently put Clinton to Obama’s left. Clinton had already come out in favor of killing the Keystone XL pipeline by the time that Obama did it, for example. If he’d rejected the idea of an executive action approach to immigration and climate, I don’t think that would have stopped her from embracing them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The basic dilemma Democrats faced in the 2016 cycle was that the normal trajectory is for public opinion to become more conservative with a Democrat in the White House. This is why pulling off the presidential three-peat is very challenging. Republicans did it in 1988 because George H.W. Bush had been the moderate factional candidate back in the 1980 primary and he was perceived, mostly accurately, as more moderate than Ronald Reagan. By offering voters a chance at a recalibration toward the center that didn’t require voting for a Democrat, the Republicans won four more years in power and really entrenched Reagan’s legacy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It looked at one point like Democrats might pull the same thing off with Clinton. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>She was seen as more moderate than Obama in the 2008 primary, her husband’s administration had been more moderate than Obama’s, and in the 2014 midterm cycle she and Bill were in-demand surrogates for vulnerable Democrats terrified of the then-unpopular president. But the basic problem is that while public opinion got more conservative in Obama’s second term, the appetite of the Democrats’ interest group infrastructure got larger. The groups, in essence, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d090a443-d185-4b27-a470-6db69206d587?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">were escaping the veal pen</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the extent that there was an avoidable error in all this, I believe it was the Clinton camp overreacting to the tie in the Iowa caucuses by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/880582f1-972d-4739-951e-a50f16103661?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">getting to Bernie Sanders’s left on identity issues</a><span>. I don’t think there is any evidence that this strategy actually worked against Sanders in the primary and it made it very hard for her to spend the general election season suggesting she was maybe a bit more of an old-school Democrat than Obama. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Ben Frustuck:</a><span> This week Jay Caspian Kang got into it with you on Twitter. Previously, this happened with John Ganz. Both these writers seem like they would be pretty simpatico with you (willing to criticize the left from the point of view of some of its own ideals) and also seems like you’re fairly supportive of them. What’s your explanation of their pushback? Question of intended audience? Fear of being seen as politically conventional? Something about the legacy of data journalism?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think Kang and Ganz are both pretty smart, insightful writers whose work I enjoy even if I don’t always agree with them. But they both tend to discuss me, personally, in ways that I find extremely unfair and annoying. As you say, they are both very happy to engage in critical scrutiny of the left and of the left’s projects in a way that I find valuable and in many respects congenial. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The risk when you’re a smart and insightful writer who’s willing to engage in criticism of left political projects is that you may find yourself getting kicked out of the gang. One way to try to avoid that — or perhaps just to reassure yourself that you still belong in the gang — is to go out and be a jerk to me, who is definitely not in the gang. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At any rate that’s my speculation. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=289935032" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Tim Nichols:</a><span> </span><span>I’d like an updated list of recommendations for donations in advance of the midterms.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Working on it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=288967701" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Lea:</span></a><span> I first went to Costco over a year ago and it has low key changed my life. Amazing shopping experience. Great quality of products. Clean, orderly store. I can eat healthier for cheap. I can host parties more cheaply. It’s fun to go there. And so I started watching business news on Costco and turns out they pay their workers really well AND return substantial dividends to stockholders. They minimize markups and encourage high employee retention. They think long term and minimize per-unit profits to maximize long term value and customer loyalty. Is there a way public policy can encourage more businesses to operate like Costco? It’s truly amazing how they serve everyone involved with the company so well and also make lots of money. Is there any way federal rules could encourage businesses to value employees and think long term? My first thoughts are a higher minimum wage or change publicly traded companies reporting requirements so that profits are reported every six months rather than every three. Doubt that would just magically create more Costco-like behavior in American business, but it would be nice for Costco Thought to proliferate.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think the basic tightness of the labor market is an important consideration here along with the minimum wage. When the government acts to keep the unemployment rate consistently low, that encourages managers to think about employee retention and high productivity. When the government allows high unemployment to linger (as it did from 2002–15), that encourages a management focus on squeezing workers. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The one thing I’d flag about Costco is that while I love it to death, you can see that the warehouses have relatively few employees per square foot compared to a normal supermarket. If you need help finding something, you’ll have trouble flagging someone down. That’s part of the business model. The employees are well-compensated, but the whole enterprise is structured around using labor somewhat sparsely relative to the overall scale of the stores. By the same token, the stores are enormous and require an incredibly wide intake zone of potential customers. I’m currently in Hancock County, Maine, hours away from the closest Costco and with no prospect of one opening up anywhere near here any time soon. So while I think Costco is great, it’s not necessarily a model for how everything could work. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e0d65383-2495-47e9-8bb2-51ce889e4b38?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>David Muccigrosso:</span></a><span> Haley Stevens is emblematic of the core failure mode in Matt’s recent way of thinking: We keep trying to force *losers* like her onto the primary electorate, then we panic when they predictably lose the primary or general, and blame the left for the loss either way.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This is a great model for never having to accept blame, but a bad model for actually winning elections.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I think it’s pretty obvious that McMorrow was the strongest general election candidate, and simply got squeezed out between two camps who would’ve otherwise been OK with her. In an RCV primary, she probably wins out.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So I ask Matt, what do we as a party need to do to empower the McMorrows who can actually win elections, instead of foisting the Stevenses on voters who don’t actually understand Median Voter Theorem?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Begging everyone to read the articles — I want to flag that I said the following in my </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a10ae567-9ba9-4b35-a914-54c9950189d1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>September 2025 preview of the election map</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #04B2A5;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The state I’m sweating is Michigan. I’d expect a generic Democrat to beat a generic Republican in a Trump midterm climate in this purple state. But the left is making a strong play to win this nomination with Abdul El-Sayed, who’s a very nice, very smart person, but I just see no reason to think that voters in this slightly red state are particularly excited about an unusually left-wing Democrat.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make matters worse, the party establishment decided to line up behind Haley Stevens as the electable alternative. Stevens is an unremarkable mainstream House Democrat on ideology, but she has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbbd632b-74ac-4a9a-81a0-79a74c92e07c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">literally the worst wins-above-replacement (WAR) rating</a><span> among the six House Democrats from Michigan. You guys know that I think </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9bafa972-6bd3-4536-a8be-9ee02103406e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">moderation and policy positioning are incredibly important</a><span>, but they’re not </span><em>all</em><span> that matters in politics and Stevens is literally a worse performer than Rashida Tlaib.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a result, I said my favorite was the third horse in the race Mallory McMorrow. And note that there was a long stretch of time when </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cbf2f361-788f-44f0-a438-c395ae786d7b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">McMorrow was But obviously Gretchen Whitmer would have been the ideal choice here. I think Kristen McDonald Rivet would have been a sounder electability pick among the House delegation and former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan would have been an interesting option, but he chose to launch an independent bid for governor that he abandoned. #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Glenn Dunmire:</a><span> </span><span>In last weeks mailbag you said in response to a question about increasing House terms to four years (and I am paraphrasing): “there are reforms that are a good idea but not worth dedicating resources to.” So that begs the question, what are some reforms that do seem worthwhile to pursue and put resources behind? For example, I would argue keeping the Electoral College but making states allot electors proportional to the popular vote is a reform worth putting some effort behind. Curious as to what your take(s) would be.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The big kahuna of worthwhile political reform is to end gerrymandering as a problem by using proportional representation. For House elections, that’s easy: Just make a national rule. For state legislatures, it’s tougher because you’re not going to want to unilaterally disarm in the states you control, but hopefully something can be worked out. Proportional representation naturally facilitates the rise of multi-party politics, but that raises the question of how to handle elections for single offices (Senate, governor, etc.). The answer is fusion voting — politicians in those races should be allowed to seek the endorsement of more than one party. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=288933788" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>EC-2021: </span></a><span>I was fiddling around with some stuff and was thinking about two related phenomena of oppositional reading (that is reading the text in opposition to its intended meaning) and I think I’ve noticed a sorta weird pattern? Both the right and the left do this (see e.g. ‘Zootopia is secretly racist’ and ‘the true Red Pill is waking up from liberal brainwashing’) but the pattern I’ve noticed is that the left seems to take something that is supposed to be progressive and decries it as secretly rightist, while the right attempts to coopt something popular and say that it’s secretly rightist, or proves their point, or whatever? Is this a real pattern, or am I letting my annoyance with folks make me overread?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Isn’t this just downstream of the fact that to the extent that contemporary pop-culture figures overtly espouse political views, they tend to be progressive? It would be funny to find an exception and try to do an against-the-grain leftist reading of “Citizen Vigilante” or something. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=288764226" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Max Haas:</a><span> </span><span>I basically agree with AOC on policy I want enacted, but am fully Yglesias-pilled on how I believe politics in America actually functions. Given that, who’s the sort of candidate I should look to in the next presidential election?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say it’s 2008. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You’re in your early 20s. You think the Iraq War was a huge mistake, you believe in same-sex marriage equality and marijuana legalization, and you also think a Canadian-style health-care system would be good. Should you vote in the primary for Barack Obama, who agrees with you about item one, disagrees about two and three, and has said he kind of agrees with you about four in principle but doesn’t think it’s realistic, so he’s proposing something much more modest? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Well, that’s not just a hypothetical — it’s how I felt in 2008, and it’s how all my friends felt. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the time, absolutely nobody thought there was a serious case that instead of voting for Obama we should try to find someone who was going to run on single-payer, gay marriage, and marijuana legalization. Suppose we’d gotten a nominee like that. And suppose he was very charismatic and media savvy and also benefited from strong economic fundamentals in 2008 and actually won the election. Well, he would have won fewer states than Obama. Say goodbye to Indiana, North Carolina, Virginia, and Florida on that map. Democrats would have picked up fewer Senate seats. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And for what? To pick a legislative fight over marriage equality that was doomed? So that you could pass a health-care bill that was narrower and did less than the Affordable Care Act? To make it harder to get Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan on the Supreme Court? What would the point of that have been? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing I just find incredibly vexing about the post-Obama left is that it’s hard to tell what “agree with A.O.C. on policy” actually means. What are her priorities? What does she think is important? How does she envision building a just national economy while Republicans totally monopolize political power across 20 states indefinitely? But I raise these questions not as an indictment of her as an individual but as an indictment of the larger left ecosystem that she’s part of. Because it’s not just that she would never in a million years embrace Obama-level pragmatism on cultural issues; neither would Gavin Newsom. The conventional wisdom about how to conduct politics has changed for the worse. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The whole concept of what it means to be engaged in the political process has become </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1cbdf17b-2a5a-4fb6-8e63-a4072fac0e5e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>much more expressive</span></a><span> to the point where I don’t really understand what elected officials are trying to do or what they want me to think of them exactly. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-da8?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=288710544" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Oliver:</span></a><span> Do you think that much of the public is unaware of Ottoman, Barbary, Korean, Roman, Arab, Byzantine slavery etc and that influences their view on American slavery? There seem to be genuine surprise when other slave owning societies are mentioned in discourse.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Clearly the mass public is just broadly unaware of any kinds of facts about the history of foreign countries. So I think it’s both true that the public is unaware of the extensive Ottoman slave trade but also that this isn’t particularly remarkable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you push a progressive intellectual on this point, they will tell you that Ottoman slavery was not foundational to the economy in the way that Western Hemisphere plantation economies were based on enslaved labor. So then you might note that 19th-century American plantation economies actually had a lot in common with the unfree labor on 19th-century Russian plantation economies. But the counterpoint is that while serfs were “bound to the land,” they were not chattel who could be sold off as individuals; they were simply sold as part of whole estates. So you end up with a lot of wrangling where every specific aspect of American slavery has close parallels elsewhere, but no other system is exactly the same. But that kind of taxonomy misses the point. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s notably distinctive about American slavery is that most foreign slave societies were chock-a-block with illiberalism and exploitative economic relationships, while early 19th-century America had made incredible moral and political progress and yet maintained this barbaric system of forced labor through the first two generations of the Republic. That’s a remarkable fact about American history: We had this great Enlightenment revolution and wrote the Declaration of Independence and still went forward with slavery. Absolutely nothing the Ottomans or Tsarist Russia did aligns with modern ideas of freedom and equality, so the forced labor doesn’t stick out like a sore thumb in the same way. But people are confusing the figure and the ground when they see American slavery as exceptional. What’s exceptional is the Declaration of Independence but then slavery was the exception to the exception.  </span></p><p class="button-wrapper"
