</a><span>on America’s 250-year anniversary, I argued that respect for the individual was the “secret sauce” in the U.S.’ long-lasting preeminence among nations. But it was certainly not the only factor. There were plenty of institutional innovations that helped the U.S. stay on top — economically, militarily, and in terms of the attractiveness of its society. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of these was American science. Today we take things like the modern research university, government grants for science, public-to-private research spinoffs, etc. for granted, but a lot of that infrastructure wasn’t there before World War 2. It was either invented or scaled up massively by the U.S. government in the postwar period, led by far-sighted scientist-bureaucrats like Vannevar Bush (pictured above). If you want to read about this history, a good place to start would be Jonathan Gruber and Simon Johnson’s excellent book </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/110f722c-5695-4a7c-9e3f-e926d8de1103?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Jump-Starting America</a></em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Those scientific institutions didn’t exist in a vacuum, however. They were backed by the U.S. government’s abiding faith in the power of science — and, even more fundamentally, by deep popular trust in the scientific enterprise. Science gave us radar and the atom bomb in wartime, and in peacetime it gave us plastics, vaccines, cheap food, and a thousand other things that made our lives easier. Science was also the driver behind American industry — chemicals, aerospace, telecommunications, computers, electronics, and so on. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We owed science our jobs, our livelihoods, our comfortable living standards, and our greatness and power as a nation. It’s little wonder that both political parties, even as they fought viciously over other issues, were steadfast in their support of science. For a long time, the only people who distrusted science were a hippie fringe on the left who disliked modernity (or thought they did, anyway), who also disliked American industry and American power, and who subscribed to an early version of degrowth environmentalism.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>America’s scientific enterprise is still strong, especially compared to the systems in Europe, Japan, Korea, and other developed countries. It has lost a lot of ground to China in a relative sense, but a lot of that is because of China’s incredible growth; as China has poured untold amounts of money and talent into its research labs, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd96d8a6-bb1d-4557-a4f5-13775fdefc31?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">spending</a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf39b2a3-e9d0-4011-be7b-12683b999b2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">output</a><span> have overtaken the U.S. by some measures. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a few ways in which China’s rise creates problems for American science — for example, top scientists can choose to work in China instead of in the U.S. — and of course there’s the concern that China’s technological strength will help its </span><em>military</em><span> to reign supreme. But overall, China’s rise in science should be </span><em>good</em><span> for American science, since American scientists can use Chinese discoveries for free and build on them. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The much bigger problem is that the scientific enterprise America built during and after World War 2 is now being threatened with </span><em>absolute</em><span> decline. The biggest problem, of course, is that much of the country — the Republican half — has basically lost faith in the scientific enterprise. To what degree this loss of faith is justified is an open question, and deserves to be discussed openly. But the larger point — that the system that powered American dominance is under threat — is true either way. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Most Americans still trust science, but MAGA Republicans don’t</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a myth, popular in right-wing circles, that scientists have lost the trust of regular Americans — either due to the increasingly left-wing composition of academic departments, or to misbehavior during Covid, or to DEI-related research taking over science, etc. This also fits with a wider narrative that Americans are losing trust in all of our institutions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it just isn’t true. Poll after poll shows that on the whole, Americans still trust scientists and want to spend more on science. For example, here’s a Pew poll from late 2025 showing that although about a fifth of Republicans did lose confidence in science in 2020, two thirds still have at least “a fair amount” of Whatever left-wing politicization of science happened during the Biden administration — and there was definitely some of that — it was not enough to make most Republicans lose faith in the scientific enterprise, or favor research cuts in order to purge unwanted ideology from the system. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That doesn’t mean I think progressives should continue down </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/115abd24-ef94-4e7d-9574-8ca2991502f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the path of politicizing scientific research</a><span>. They should not, and Biden made real missteps in this area.  Objectivity clearly matters for public trust of science in the long term. But as of right now, there’s no crisis of trust in science, except among the smallish minority of people who are running around screaming that there’s a crisis of trust in science.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But despite science’s overwhelming popularity and public trust, Trump and his administration are launching an unprecedented and devastating attack on American science — cutting funding, and forcing science projects to undergo ideological review by government commissars. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Trump’s comprehensive attack on science</h4><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When Trump proposed cuts to federal science spending in his first term, a whole bunch of people — Yours Truly included — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/578bd059-60c5-49b9-8bc4-b32f70fe17f1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">shouted very loudly</a><span> that this would be a bad idea. There was even a (slightly cheesy) </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6fb58250-a65e-4a7d-8478-77804d8cd7ff?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">March for Science</a><span> to oppose the cuts. I don’t think we were crying wolf at that point; instead, the defenders of science harnessed the fading embers of the bipartisan consensus to successfully stop the cuts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The pattern has been that in his second term, Trump has done many of the things he merely threatened to do in his first. #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Trump administration has proposed a rule</a><span> that all federal scientific grants should have to pass a political review by government operatives. That sounds like it must be an exaggeration, and I wish it were. But here’s how Alex Tabarrok — who is no one’s idea of either a lefty or an alarmist — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38ad3640-ee27-4569-9792-881a88af0655?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">describes the Trump proposal</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OMB, joined by some forty grantmaking agencies—NSF, HHS, DOE, NASA, DOD among them—has proposed a sweeping rewrite of the rules governing all federal grants…Program goals must now be “</span><strong><span>aligned with administration policies and priorities</span></strong><span>”…Merit review is subordinated to politics: “senior appointees must conduct these reviews,” ensuring “that discretionary awards </span><strong><span>advance the President’s policy priorities</span></strong><span>,” while “peer review remains advisory and does not replace agency discretion”…And every grant becomes terminable at will, whenever it “no longer effectuates program goals, Federal agency priorities, or the national interest *as they exist at the time of the termination*”…Universities must even ensure their subrecipients don’t “significantly damage the reputation of… the Federal Government”…a loyalty clause for scientists…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Political review of every award, peer review demoted, agency review promoted, termination whenever “priorities” change. Chilling. It’s a nightmare of petty low-trust review of the kind that is already drowning science…One dial in the White House now turns every grant program in the country. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rule hasn’t yet been formally adopted, but Trump </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/26dd0b91-df0b-4e50-a05f-0aba9dd17980?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">issued an executive order in 2025</a><span> that has already implemented political review of many grants. This is undoubtedly a big reason for the delays and cuts. Essentially, the Trump administration is conducting a thoroughgoing political purge of all government science funding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If there’s still any doubt that this is a political purge, here’s what Trump’s people wrote in the proposed new rule:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the previous administration, executive agencies frequently chose to subsidize and expressly </span><strong>prioritize projects based on their ideological alignment</strong><span>…If executive agencies were entitled to subsidize those types of activities during the previous administration, there is no constitutional basis to prevent the government from reaching a different policy determination regarding which activities to fund during this administration. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In other words, the Biden administration funded a bunch of research that Trump’s people don’t like — especially DEI-related stuff. So now, in retaliation, Trump’s people are going to review every single science grant and cut out the stuff they don’t like. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But instead of making it a one-time purge, they’re </span><em>institutionalizing</em><span> the idea — they’re making it so that from now on, in perpetuity, all federal science grants have to pass political review. Presumably, that rule will continue to hold under future Democratic administrations as well. It represents the permanent forced politicization of the scientific enterprise in America.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nor is this the only way Trump is attacking American science. He’s also making it much harder for foreign researchers to study and work in America. And between the political purges, the new science commissars, and the attacks on skilled immigration, America under Trump is looking more and more like the authoritarian regimes that the scientists of previous decades would come to America in order to escape. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">How worried should we be?</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The next question is how worried we should be about Trump’s attack on American science. Some people talk about the issue in very dramatic terms. Here’s Ross Andersen in </span><em>The Atlantic</em><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every scientific empire falls</span><span>, but not at the same speed, or for the same reasons…Some civilizations have willfully squandered their scientific advantage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Spanish science, for example, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4a375b44-9a2d-453a-bd2b-43c862431379?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">suffered</a><span> grievously during the Inquisition…In the 17th century, the Spanish made almost no contribution to the ongoing Scientific Revolution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Soviets sabotaged their own success in biomedicine. In the 1920s, the U.S.S.R. had one of the most advanced genetics programs in the world, but that was before Stalin </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/606a4562-8d2b-4f41-939e-6847b368d958?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">empowered Trofim Lysenko</a><span>, a political appointee….Some of the scientists were tossed into the Gulag; others starved or faced firing squads. As a consequence of all this, the Soviets played no role in the discovery of DNA’s double-helix structure…[T]he U.S.S.R. was a generation behind in molecular biology and couldn’t catch up.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it was Adolf Hitler who possessed the greatest talent for scientific self-harm. Germany had been a great scientific power going back to the late 19th century…When the Nazis took over in 1933, Hitler purged Germany’s universities of Jewish professors and others who opposed his rule. Many scientists were murdered. Others fled the country…In a very short time, the center of gravity for science just up and moved across the Atlantic Ocean.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As far as those historical examples go, this isn’t alarmism. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f2918533-98df-47fc-884e-5cf96c050304?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Waldinger (2016)</a><span> looks at the impact of Nazi firings of Jewish scientists on German and Austrian science departments. He finds that kicking out scientists was extremely damaging to scientific output, and that the damage lasted for at least 50 years without healing. Those same Jewish scientists, of course, mostly went to the U.S., and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53c2dce9-4ac6-4c04-af62-5cfb5582928e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">gave a huge boost to American science</a><span> during and long after the war.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today, it’s Chinese scientists who form the single most crucial global talent pool — and the pool that America is losing most rapidly. One obvious example is AI — undoubtedly the most important area of research right now. According to recent data, fully 38% of top AI researchers were educated in the People’s Republic — a bigger percent than any other nation:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static"
